newsitem.title: AUSTRALIA: CANBERRA WATCH - Progress in the Senate.
newsitem.headline: CANBERRA WATCH - Progress in the Senate.

text.p: The government has issued its habitually optimistic programme for the Senate for next week.
The programme envisages:
-- Completion of the Workplace Relations and Other Legislation Amendment Bill (the prosaic title of the government's new labour system);
-- Progress on the Telstra (Dilution of Public Ownership) Bill; and
-- The entry into the Senate of the first of the budget bills: the family tax initiative and the appropriations bills.
But let's not get our hopes up.
The most progress that can probably be expected is that the industrial relations bill might be completed.
Telstra certainly will not be finished and probably the budget bills won't be either. The budget bills are not too important anyway.
Understanding Senate process is the key to monitoring developments next week.

A bill is "read" three times. The first reading is a formality, the second is the main debate and the third finally indicates assent. Between the second and third readings, a bill will normally be sent off "to committee", which is actually the whole Senate operating in an amendment mode.

This is the stage that the industrial relations bill has reached. It was read a first time some time ago. Last week the second reading debate was finished and the bill was sent to committee. The committee stage is next week.
Since the bill is expected to pass in some form or another, the devil will be in the detail of the Democrats' amendments.
(Ignore the other players; for this bill the Democrats are the most co-operative source of the two votes that the government needs.)
So next week will probably bring the real decision on the new industrial relations system, and the result will emerge piecemeal as successive amendments are inserted into the bill.
But Senate sources tell Reuters that the industrial relations bill will may take up the entire week.
But the other items on the government schedule are not too important, anyway.
Telstra bill is only supposed to be dealt with for referral to committee; it wasn't going to be decided.
The family fax initiative bills are additional spending, not spending cuts or revenue rises. So it matters little whether they pass or not (ignoring the beneficiaries for the moment).
And the appropriations bills must pass.
These are the legislative cheques by which the government is authorised to draw money from the treasury to run the country.
They must pass in exactly the form that the government has introduced them, and they certainly will by the end of the year, even if the Senate goes through the motions of asking for changes.
-- Canberra Bureau 61-6 273-2730
